lessons.title: Ask a research question and get a citation-backed answer in ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Write focused, scoped questions that make ChatGPT's web search return answers with real, checkable citations instead of a generic AI narrative.
lessons.goal: Ask a specific research question in ChatGPT with web search on and get an answer where every claim traces to a clickable, dated source.
lessons.whyItMatters: ChatGPT can answer purely from training data, which means a confident-sounding paragraph with nothing to check. Turning on web search changes that: GPT-5.6 decides when to search, or you can force it, and the response comes back with clickable source links instead of an unattributed narrative. That only pays off if you ask questions specific and scoped enough to pull real sources instead of a generic summary. This is the habit every other lesson in this course builds on.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A ChatGPT account (Free or Plus) at chatgpt.com or the app. Free's GPT-5.3 Instant tier can search the web too, but Plus and Go tiers get higher search limits and GPT-5.6 Sol, which searches more reliably on ambiguous questions.
steps: Open a new chat in ChatGPT and click the search icon in the composer to force a web search, rather than trusting the model to decide on its own.
Write one specific question, not a broad topic — name the exact fact, comparison, or figure you need.
Add scope constraints: timeframe, geography, and the kind of source you want prioritized.
Read the answer next to its inline citations — small clickable source links attached to the claims they support.
Click through 2-3 of the citations to confirm the source actually supports what's claimed.
Ask a tight follow-up in the same chat to narrow or extend the answer rather than starting a new one.
lessons.prompt: I need a fact-based answer with citations, not general knowledge. Search the web for this — do not answer from what you already know. Question: [YOUR SPECIFIC QUESTION]. Scope: prioritize sources from [timeframe, e.g. the last 12 months] and favor [source type, e.g. primary sources, regulatory filings, industry reports] for [geography/market]. If sources disagree, tell me explicitly and show both positions with their citations. Do not state anything you cannot attribute to a source.
lessons.explanation: Naming the exact fact you need, instead of a topic, is what triggers a targeted search instead of a synthesized general-knowledge paragraph. Explicitly telling ChatGPT to search rather than rely on what it already knows matters because it will otherwise answer fluently from training data with no citations at all. The timeframe and source-type constraints stop it from blending an old blog post in with this week's news. The 'if sources disagree' clause matters because a confident single answer often hides real disagreement between sources — asking for it explicitly surfaces that disagreement instead of letting ChatGPT quietly pick one side.
lessons.example:
Weak: "Tell me about EU data residency rules."

Strong: "Search the web for this. What are the current data residency requirements for storing EU customer data, and have there been any regulatory changes in the last 12 months? Scope: prioritize official EU/national regulator sources over law-firm blog summaries. If sources disagree on interpretation, show both."

The strong version returns a short, sourced answer citing the actual regulation and any recent amendments, with dates attached — something you could put in front of a compliance lead without a follow-up round of "but is this current?"
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, take a real question from your work this week and rewrite it using the scoped prompt template above with web search on.
lessons.expectedResult: An answer with three or more clickable citations, where you've opened at least two of them and confirmed they say what the answer claims.
commonMistakes: Asking a broad topic question ("tell me about X industry") and getting a generic, hard-to-verify narrative pulled from training data instead of a sourced answer.
Not explicitly telling ChatGPT to search the web, so it answers fluently from memory with nothing to click.
Never clicking a citation, so you're trusting ChatGPT's summary of the source instead of the source itself.
Leaving out a timeframe and getting an answer that mixes current facts with outdated ones without flagging which is which.
lessons.proTip: For a question where being wrong is costly, run the same scoped question through Claude's web search as an independent second read — different retrieval, different sources, and agreement across both tools is a stronger signal than either alone.

lessons.title: Verify ChatGPT's citations before you trust or forward them
lessons.summary: Build a quick habit of checking that a citation actually supports the claim it's attached to, catching weak sources before they end up in your work.
lessons.goal: Check any ChatGPT web-search answer you plan to rely on by confirming each key claim is directly supported by its cited source, not just adjacent to it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Citations lower the risk of AI hallucination, but they don't remove it — ChatGPT can attach a source that's tangentially related rather than truly supportive, or cite a low-quality outlet with the same confident tone as a primary source. Professionals who forward research to a client, boss, or investor need a fast verification routine, not blind trust in the presence of a link.
steps: After getting a web-search answer, list the specific claims you actually plan to rely on or repeat elsewhere.
Open the citation attached to each of those claims.
Check whether the source states the claim directly or only implies something close to it.
Check the source's publication date and type — primary source, reputable outlet, or unverified aggregator.
Flag any claim resting on a single weak or old source as risky to repeat as-is.
For flagged claims, ask ChatGPT to search again for a second, independent source before you rely on the figure.
Keep a short note of what you verified alongside any research you pass on to someone else.
lessons.prompt: Show your source for every factual claim in your last answer. For each claim, quote the exact sentence from the cited source that supports it. If a claim isn't directly supported by a quotable sentence in any source, say so explicitly instead of leaving it unmarked.
lessons.explanation: Asking ChatGPT to quote the exact supporting sentence forces a self-audit: a claim it can quote cleanly is well-grounded, while a claim it can only loosely paraphrase from the source is the one worth double-checking yourself. This catches the common failure mode where an answer sounds precise but the underlying source was actually broader or vaguer than the claim implied.
lessons.example: Research question: "What's the average B2B SaaS churn rate?" ChatGPT cites an industry report for a specific percentage. Running the verification prompt reveals the report's number is specific to enterprise SaaS with 500+ employee customers — ChatGPT had generalized it to "B2B SaaS" broadly. Catching this before quoting the figure in a pricing memo avoids repeating an overstated claim.
lessons.exercise: Take an answer from the previous lesson (or a fresh research question), run the verification prompt on it, and find at least one claim that turns out to be weaker or narrower than it first appeared.
lessons.expectedResult: You can point to one specific claim in a ChatGPT answer and say, with a quoted sentence, exactly how well-supported (or unsupported) it actually is.
commonMistakes: Treating a high citation count as proof of quality — ten citations can still mean zero truly independent confirmations of the specific claim you care about.
Not checking publication dates, so a "current" answer turns out to lean on a source from several years ago.
Accepting a citation from a low-quality aggregator site with the same confidence as a primary source or regulator filing.
Forwarding research to a client or decision-maker without having verified the claims that actually matter to the decision.
lessons.proTip: For high-stakes numbers — financial, legal, regulatory — ask Gemini the same question with Deep Research and check whether its independently retrieved sources land on the same figure.

lessons.title: Run focused market research for a real business decision with Gemini Deep Research
lessons.summary: Break a pending business decision into sourced sub-questions and run each as its own Gemini Deep Research brief, then compile the results into a short, defensible decision brief.
lessons.goal: Turn a specific business decision into a set of sourced Gemini Deep Research runs and compile the results into a one-page decision brief.
lessons.whyItMatters: Decisions like market entry, pricing changes, or targeting a new segment need current, fragmented data pulled together fast — manually searching dozens of sources is slow, and a vague AI prompt just produces a generic overview nobody can act on. Anchoring the research to the actual decision, with sources and dates on every number, gives you something you can defend in the room.
steps: Write down the actual decision you're making, not just the topic — "should we launch a $49/mo tier", not "SaaS pricing."
Break the decision into 3-4 sub-questions Gemini Deep Research can each answer with real data (market size, competitor pricing, demand signals, constraints).
In the Gemini app, choose Deep Research from the tools menu and run each sub-question as its own focused brief rather than one giant, vague prompt.
Review the research plan Gemini proposes before it starts browsing, and edit it if a sub-question is missing an angle you need.
Require a source and a date on every number or claim in the report, not narrative summaries.
Cross-check any figure you plan to put in a deck against a second source.

Compile the sourced reports into a short decision brief, exporting to Google Docs and keeping citations attached, and note anything Gemini couldn't answer confidently so you can flag it for another research method.
lessons.prompt: I'm making this business decision: [DECISION, e.g. "whether to launch a $49/month starter tier for our project management SaaS targeting small agencies"]. Research question: [SPECIFIC SUB-QUESTION, e.g. "What do the 5 leading project management SaaS tools charge for their entry-level paid tier, and what features are included at that price?"]. For each one, give me: name, price, billing period, key included features, and the source with its publication date. Only include pricing you can verify is currently active — flag anything that might be outdated.
lessons.explanation: Naming the actual decision keeps every sub-question tied to something you'll act on, instead of drifting into a generic industry overview that reads well but doesn't move the decision forward. Splitting the decision into sub-questions and running each as its own Deep Research brief produces sharper answers than one sprawling prompt trying to cover everything at once. Requiring a source and date per data point is what turns the output from "the AI said so" into something you can defend in a meeting.
lessons.example: Decision: should a boutique consulting firm raise its hourly rate. Sub-questions run as separate Deep Research briefs: current market rate ranges for similar consulting by specialty and region, findings from recent industry rate surveys, and the inflation-adjusted rate trend over the past three years. The three sourced reports compile into a short table — rate range, source, date — that goes straight into the partner's pricing decision memo.
lessons.exercise: Pick a real business decision pending at your job, break it into three sub-questions, run each one as a Gemini Deep Research brief in your own account, and compile a one-page sourced brief.
lessons.expectedResult: A short brief with at least three data points directly relevant to the decision, each traceable to a dated, clickable source.
commonMistakes: Researching the general topic instead of the specific decision, producing an unusable overview.
Asking for numbers without requiring dates, so 2022 and 2026 figures end up mixed together unknowingly.
Approving Gemini's research plan without reading it, so a sub-question quietly runs with the wrong angle.
Never writing down which sub-questions Gemini couldn't answer confidently, so gaps get discovered too late.
lessons.proTip: If your decision depends on internal context too, turn on Deep Research's Workspace grounding so it pulls relevant Gmail threads and Drive docs alongside the public web, without you manually uploading anything.

lessons.title: Build a repeatable competitor analysis workflow in ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Use one identical Deep Research prompt template per competitor, saved inside a ChatGPT Project, so the sourced results are genuinely comparable and easy to refresh on a schedule.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured, sourced competitor comparison covering positioning, pricing, and recent moves, using a Deep Research template you can rerun for any competitor set.
lessons.whyItMatters: Competitive intel goes stale fast and usually lives scattered across old sales calls and someone's memory. A repeatable, cited Deep Research template lets marketers, consultants, and business owners refresh a competitor comparison in minutes with sources attached, instead of days of manual digging that's outdated again in a quarter.
steps: List the exact competitors and the specific dimensions to compare: positioning, pricing, target customer, recent moves.
Create a ChatGPT Project for this competitor set so every research chat shares the same custom instructions and files.
Run one Deep Research report per competitor using an identical prompt template so the answers are directly comparable.
Ask ChatGPT for a combined comparison table across all competitors once each has been researched individually.
Request "recent moves" (last 3-6 months) as its own explicit ask, since this is the most time-sensitive part.
Click through the citation for any competitive claim that would actually change your strategy.
Re-run the same Deep Research prompts quarterly, or before major decisions, inside the same Project to keep the comparison current.
lessons.prompt: Research [COMPETITOR NAME] as a competitor to [YOUR COMPANY/PRODUCT]. Give me, with a source and date for each: 1) current positioning/tagline and target customer, 2) pricing tiers and what's included, 3) any product launches, pricing changes, or funding news in the last 6 months, 4) publicly stated strengths and weaknesses from reviews or analyst coverage, not your own opinion. Keep sourced facts separate from any inference — mark inferred statements clearly as "inference" rather than fact.
lessons.explanation: Using an identical prompt for every competitor is what makes the outputs genuinely comparable in a table later, instead of three differently-shaped write-ups that resist being placed side by side. Isolating "recent moves" as its own explicit ask matters because a general "tell me about X" query tends to surface older, better-indexed content over last week's actual news. The fact/inference split stops sourced data and analyst opinion from blending together as if they carried equal weight.
lessons.example: Ahead of a positioning refresh, a marketer runs the identical template as three separate Deep Research reports inside one ChatGPT Project, then asks ChatGPT to "combine these three reports into one comparison table." The result is a source-linked table — positioning, pricing, last-6-months moves — ready to paste directly into a strategy document.
lessons.exercise: Pick 2-3 real competitors, run the template prompt as a Deep Research report for each in your own ChatGPT account, then ask for a combined comparison table.
lessons.expectedResult: A comparison table covering every listed competitor, with a citation attached to each pricing claim and each "recent move" claim.
commonMistakes: Writing a different prompt for each competitor, which makes the results impossible to compare fairly afterward.
Skipping the "last 6 months" filter and getting a mix of current and years-old positioning presented as equally current.
Treating reviews or analyst opinion as objective fact instead of marking it clearly as inference.
Running this once and never refreshing it, so the comparison quietly goes stale within a quarter.
lessons.proTip: Set the Project's custom instructions to always require a source and date per claim, so you don't have to retype that constraint into every new Deep Research brief.

lessons.title: Generate a long-form report with Gemini Deep Research
lessons.summary: Write a scoped research brief instead of a one-line question so Gemini Deep Research returns a structured, cited report you can actually act on.
lessons.goal: Run a well-scoped Deep Research brief in Gemini and get a multi-section, cited report matching your requested structure, not a shallow generic overview.
lessons.whyItMatters: Some questions need dozens or hundreds of sources synthesized — market landscape reports, due diligence, industry primers — not a quick answer. Deep Research automates a multi-hour research task into minutes and is free on Gemini's Flash tier for everyone, so each run deserves the same care as a real research assignment, not a casual question typed on the fly.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Google account signed into the Gemini app (gemini.google.com or the mobile app). Deep Research runs on the free tier; Google AI Pro or Ultra raises your daily quota and runs the report on the Gemini 3.1 Pro model, with a "Deep Research Max" tier for the heaviest reports.
steps: Open the Gemini app and select Deep Research from the tools menu before you start typing.
Write a brief, not a question: scope, audience, what decision the report will inform, and what to exclude.
Review the research plan Gemini drafts — edit any step or add a missing sub-topic before you approve it.
Click Start research and expect several minutes while it browses and synthesizes sources.
Read the full report, not just the summary, and skim the source list for obvious quality issues.
Ask targeted follow-ups to expand thin sections or add a section you needed but didn't get.
Export the report to Google Docs and keep the source list attached for anyone who will act on it.
lessons.prompt: Write a research report on: [TOPIC]. Audience: [who will read it and why, e.g. "our leadership team deciding whether to enter the X market"]. Scope: cover [specific sub-topics, e.g. market size and growth, key players, regulatory landscape, entry barriers]. Exclude: [things out of scope, e.g. the consumer segment, regions outside the EU]. Structure the report with headed sections and end with a short "key risks and open questions" section. Cite every data point and flag any section where sources conflict or are thin.
lessons.explanation: Deep Research quality depends heavily on the brief, not the question — giving it audience and decision context lets it prioritize the sections that actually matter instead of producing a generic overview. Reviewing the research plan before approving it is your one real editing window: adjusting it there is far cheaper than re-running the whole report afterward. Requesting a "risks and open questions" section forces honesty about the report's own limits, which is exactly what makes it usable for a real decision instead of just impressive-looking.
lessons.example: A founder evaluating expansion scopes a Deep Research brief to "market size, top 5 competitors, regulatory barriers, and a realistic 3-year growth range for solar panel installation SMBs in Germany." Before approving the plan, she adds a step Gemini's draft had missed — permitting rules by German state. The finished report includes a note that "sources sometimes disagree on installer count," a caveat she circulates to leadership ahead of a go/no-go meeting rather than presenting the number as certain.
lessons.exercise: Run one real Deep Research report in your own Gemini account using a full brief, not a one-line topic, review the research plan before approving it, then read the entire report including its source list.
lessons.expectedResult: A multi-section cited report matching your requested structure, including at least one explicit "risks/open questions" or "sources disagree" note you can act on.
commonMistakes: Submitting a one-line topic instead of a scoped brief and getting back a generic, unfocused report.
Approving the research plan without reading it, missing the chance to add a sub-topic the decision actually depends on.
Skipping straight to the summary and never checking the underlying source list for quality.
Forwarding the report to a decision-maker without noting the limitations it already flagged.
lessons.proTip: Deep Research can ground itself in your Workspace content too — turn on Gmail, Chat, and Drive sources when the report needs internal context alongside the public web, with nothing to upload manually.

lessons.title: Set up a ChatGPT Project for an ongoing research project
lessons.summary: Bundle chats, uploaded documents, and custom instructions into one ChatGPT Project so a whole research project stays grounded and consistent over weeks.
lessons.goal: Create a Project with custom instructions and uploaded files so every question on a project draws on the same grounded context, and you never have to re-explain it from scratch.
lessons.whyItMatters: Research spread across disconnected chats loses context and gets re-explained every time. ChatGPT Projects bundle chats with uploaded files (up to 512MB each) and custom instructions into one workspace, and they now integrate Deep Research, memory, and Voice Mode within that same scope — so a project you're researching over weeks doesn't repeat work or drift into inconsistent findings.
steps: Create a new Project and name it for the actual project — a client name or deal, not a generic label.
Write custom instructions covering the standing context every chat in this Project should apply: industry, audience, constraints, and any angle to always check.
Upload the internal documents relevant to the project — PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV, or images — up to the Project's file limit.
Run research questions and Deep Research reports inside the Project instead of loose chats, so answers draw on both the web and your uploaded files.
Add teammates who share your workspace if you're on a Team or Enterprise plan, so they can open the same Project.
Periodically prune outdated files and refresh the custom instructions as the project evolves.
Use the Project's chat history as the running record instead of copy-pasting findings into a separate document.
lessons.prompt: This Project is for research supporting [PROJECT/CLIENT NAME]. We are a [industry/role, e.g. "boutique M&A advisory evaluating a mid-market acquisition target"]. For every question in this Project: prioritize primary sources and regulatory filings over blog commentary, always note publication dates, and flag anything relevant to [always-check angle, e.g. "regulatory or compliance risk"] even if not directly asked. When our uploaded documents contain relevant information, cite them alongside web sources and note clearly which is which.
lessons.explanation: Project-level custom instructions apply automatically to every chat started inside it, so you stop re-explaining context in every new conversation. Uploading internal files means ChatGPT can combine your own documents with fresh web citations in the same answer, clearly labeled by source type. Naming an "always-check angle" catches the risk category your team actually cares about even when an individual question forgets to ask for it directly.
lessons.example: A real estate agent creates a Project named "123 Oak St — Buyer Due Diligence," uploads the inspection report and HOA documents, and sets instructions to always flag anything relevant to permits or liens. Weeks of questions later, she opens the same Project and every new chat still reflects the same standing context — no re-briefing herself required.
lessons.exercise: Create one Project for a real ongoing project in your own account, add custom instructions, upload at least one relevant document, and run two research questions inside it.
lessons.expectedResult: A Project where a new question, asked with no repeated explanation, correctly reflects both your standing instructions and the uploaded documents.
commonMistakes: Using a single Project for everything, so instructions and files from unrelated projects bleed into each other.
Never writing custom instructions, which loses the main benefit of the Project over a plain chat.
Uploading files once and letting them go stale as the project evolves.
Keeping research in ad hoc chats out of habit instead of moving it into the Project.
lessons.proTip: On a ChatGPT Team or Enterprise workspace, Projects can be shared with teammates who have access to that workspace, so a colleague covering for you can open the same Project instead of asking you to re-explain it.

lessons.title: Turn verified ChatGPT research into a client-ready deck or spreadsheet
lessons.summary: Convert completed, checked research directly into a polished slide deck or spreadsheet using ChatGPT's data analysis tool, with sources kept intact.
lessons.goal: Take verified research and generate a structured deck or spreadsheet deliverable from it without introducing new, unverified claims.
lessons.whyItMatters: Research is only valuable once someone can act on it. ChatGPT's data analysis tool writes and runs code behind the scenes to turn a research thread into an actual downloadable file — a spreadsheet with formulas, or a slide-style document — saving the hour professionals used to lose manually reformatting bullet points into slides. The risk is generating a polished deliverable from research nobody actually checked.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A completed ChatGPT research thread (web search or Deep Research) whose key claims you've already verified, per the verification habit from earlier in this course.
steps: Verify the underlying research first — facts checked, sources confirmed — before generating any deliverable from it.
State the deliverable format explicitly: PowerPoint deck, spreadsheet, or written one-pager, plus audience and length.
Specify the structure of the deliverable — what belongs on each slide, section, or tab — rather than leaving it fully open.
Ask ChatGPT to keep citations in speaker notes, a dedicated sources slide, or a sources tab, not dropped from the final file.
Let the data analysis tool generate the actual file, then review it section-by-section against the original research thread.
Fix formatting or content gaps with a targeted follow-up rather than regenerating from scratch.
Download the file and do a final polish pass in the native app (PowerPoint, Excel) before sending.
lessons.prompt: Turn this research into a [10-slide PowerPoint deck / spreadsheet with X tabs] for [audience, e.g. "our leadership team, non-technical"]. Structure: [outline exactly what each slide/section/tab should cover, e.g. "slide 1 title, slide 2 market size, slide 3 competitor comparison table, slides 4-5 opportunities, slide 6 risks, slide 7 recommendation"]. Use your data analysis tool to generate the actual file. Keep every claim traceable — include a sources slide/tab listing the citations from the research. Do not add any claim that wasn't in the original research.
lessons.explanation: Verifying the research before generating the deliverable matters because a formatting mistake is easy to catch, but a fabricated-sounding claim buried on slide 6 of a finished deck is easy to miss — and easy to present to a client by accident. Specifying the exact structure prevents ChatGPT from choosing its own generic layout that may not fit the actual audience. Explicitly forbidding new claims stops the file-generation step from quietly introducing details that weren't in the source research.
lessons.example: A consultant runs Deep Research on outsourcing options for customer support across three regions, verifies the report's key figures, then asks for a 6-slide client deck with a sources slide, generated with the data analysis tool. After a review pass — fixing one slide where a figure needed rounding for readability — the downloaded PPTX goes to the client the same day instead of an afternoon spent rebuilding it manually in PowerPoint.
lessons.exercise: Take a research thread from earlier in this course in your own ChatGPT account, verify its key claims, and generate one deliverable (deck or spreadsheet) from it using an explicit structure.
lessons.expectedResult: A downloaded file whose content matches the verified research with no new unsupported claims, structured the way you specified rather than generically.
commonMistakes: Generating a deck straight from unverified research and only proofreading it for typos, not accuracy.
Leaving the structure open and getting a generic outline that doesn't fit the actual audience or purpose.
Letting sources disappear from the final deliverable, so no one downstream can check the claims later.
Treating the generated file as final instead of doing a last polish pass in the native app before sending.
lessons.proTip: For a deliverable type you produce regularly — a monthly market-update deck, say — save the exact structure prompt in a Project's custom instructions so future runs are a one-line paste instead of redesigning the outline every time.

lessons.title: Build a recurring Gemini research routine for your industry
lessons.summary: Design a fixed set of Deep Research questions and a Scheduled Action so you get a 15-minute sourced update on your industry every week or month, automatically, instead of starting from scratch.
lessons.goal: Set up a repeatable research routine — a fixed prompt set run on a schedule — that keeps you current on your industry without you remembering to trigger it.
lessons.whyItMatters: One-off research goes stale fast. Professionals who stay ahead run the same handful of sourced questions on a schedule — industry news, competitor moves, regulatory changes — so they walk into meetings current instead of scrambling beforehand. Gemini's Scheduled Actions turn that into a 15-minute weekly habit that runs itself, instead of a fresh research project you have to remember to start every time.
steps: Identify the 3-5 questions that actually matter to your role on a recurring basis — not everything you could research.
Write each as a reusable Deep Research brief with a placeholder for the date range, so it's a one-line edit each run.
Set up a Scheduled Action in the Gemini app so the routine runs automatically on a fixed cadence — weekly or monthly.
Ask Gemini to compare each new run to the previous one and flag what's changed since last time.
Verify anything that would actually change a decision, then pull the changed items into a short update note.
Review the routine itself quarterly — retire questions that stopped being useful, add new ones as your role changes.
lessons.prompt: Run my recurring research check for [DATE RANGE, e.g. "the last 7 days"]. Questions: 1) [e.g. "any pricing or product changes from our top 3 competitors"], 2) [e.g. "any new regulation affecting our industry in the EU"], 3) [e.g. "notable funding or M&A news in our sector"]. For each, compare to what you found in our last run and explicitly flag what's new or changed. Give me a short bulleted update, not a full report, with a citation per item.
lessons.explanation: Fixing the questions in advance is what makes the routine sustainable — deciding what to research every single time is the actual time sink, not running the search itself. A Scheduled Action is what turns the fixed prompt set into an actual habit instead of a good intention you forget by the third week. Asking for a short bulleted update instead of a full report is what keeps a 15-minute habit from quietly turning into an hour of reading each time.
lessons.example: A financial analyst sets up a Scheduled Action called "Weekly Sector Watch" with three standing questions — peer company earnings surprises, relevant regulatory announcements, and notable analyst rating changes — that runs automatically every Monday morning. Six weeks in, the "what changed" framing means reading five bullet points instead of re-reading a full market overview each week.
lessons.exercise: Define 3-4 recurring research questions relevant to your role, set up a Gemini Scheduled Action for them, and let the routine run once using the template prompt above.
lessons.expectedResult: A short, sourced, bulleted update you could act on or share in under five minutes of reading, delivered automatically from a prompt that took one line to edit.
commonMistakes: Tracking too many questions at once and abandoning the routine within a month.
Not setting up a Scheduled Action, so the routine depends on remembering to run it manually and quietly lapses.
Asking for a full report every time instead of a short delta, making the routine too slow to sustain.
Never revisiting the question list, so the routine keeps tracking things that stopped mattering to your role.
lessons.proTip: Pair this with Gemini's side panel in Gmail or Docs to turn a flagged item straight into a draft team update without leaving your inbox.
